items.prose: Takes of 1 to 3 from a pile of 26 matches. Whoever takes the last match wins, and you move first.
items.question: How many do you take?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Leave a multiple of 4.

byKey.one: Taking 1 leaves 25. Your rival takes 1 and hands you 24.
byKey.three: Taking 3 leaves 23. Your rival takes 3 and hands you 20.

explain.text: $26 = 6 \times 4 + 2$, so take 2 to leave 24. Then answer each take of $x$ with $4 - x$.

items.prose: Two players take turns to roll two dice. The first to roll a double six wins.
items.question: What is the first player's chance? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\tfrac{1}{2 - p}$ with $p = \tfrac{1}{36}$.

byKey.half: Close, but the first seat still has the first chance each round.
byKey.once: That is the chance on the first throw only.

explain.text: With $p = \tfrac{1}{36}$, the first player wins with $\tfrac{1}{2 - 1/36} = \tfrac{36}{71}$. A rare success makes the first seat worth little. As $p$ shrinks the chance tends to $\tfrac12$.

items.prose: Flip a fair coin until HTH or HHH appears.
items.question: What is the chance that HTH comes first? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use Conway's leading numbers or the node equations.

byKey.half: Same length is not the same chance.

explain.text: Take A = HTH and B = HHH. Conway's numbers are $A \cdot A = 5$, $A \cdot B = 1$, $B \cdot B = 7$ and $B \cdot A = 1$. So HHH against HTH is $(5 - 1) : (7 - 1) = 4 : 6$, and HTH wins with $\tfrac35$.

items.prose: An even-money bet wins with chance 0.52.
items.question: What is the Kelly fraction? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. At evens $f^* = p - q$.

byKey.p: That is the win chance. Subtract the loss chance.

explain.text: $f^* = 0.52 - 0.48 = 0.04$. A thin edge earns a small stake.

items.prose: A bet pays 4 to 1 and wins with chance 0.25.
items.question: What is the Kelly fraction? Give four decimal places.

byKey.evens: You used $p - q$. At 4 to 1, divide $q$ by 4.
byKey.edge: That is the edge per £1. Divide it by the odds.

explain.text: $0.25 - 0.75/4 = 0.0625$. The edge is $4 \times 0.25 - 0.75 = 0.25$ per £1, divided by the odds 4.

items.prose: You backed a team for £20 at 9 to 1. The other side is now offered at evens.
items.question: How much profit can you lock in?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $180 - h = h - 20$.

byKey.hedge: That is the hedge. The locked profit is $180 - 100$.

explain.text: $180 - h = h - 20$ gives $h = 100$. Both outcomes then pay £80.

items.prose: You want £100 on a best-of-seven series, betting game by game at evens. Your team leads 3–1.
items.question: How much do you bet on game 5?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that game 5 decides the series.

byKey.half: That is the bet at 2–2. Leading 3–1, most later results win anyway.
byKey.all: Game 5 decides the series only if games 6 and 7 would both be lost.

explain.text: Imagine games 6 and 7 played. Game 5 decides the series only if your team would lose both, chance $\tfrac14$. So bet $100 \times \tfrac14 = £25$.

items.prose: A doubler holds £15 and bets on red at a European wheel, where red wins with chance $\tfrac{18}{37}$. He doubles from £1 after each loss.
items.question: What is his expected gain per cycle? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. £15 funds four bets; use $1 - 16q^4$.

byKey.fair: That is the fair-coin answer. Red loses slightly more often than it wins.
byKey.pos: Check the sign. The rare loss outweighs the wins.

explain.text: £15 funds stakes of £1, £2, £4 and £8. With $q = \tfrac{19}{37}$, $q^4 \approx 0.06954$, so the gain is $1 - 16 \times 0.06954 \approx -0.1126$. Doubling cannot rescue an unfair game.

items.prose: An interviewer asks for the expected number of different faces in six rolls of a die.
items.question: Which idea answers it in one line?

options.text: One indicator per face, then linearity

options.why: There is no decision to make, so there is nothing to work back from.
Nothing is stopped. Optional stopping is for fair games and stopping rules.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each face contributes.

explain.text: Each face appears with chance $1 - (\tfrac56)^6$. Six indicators add to about 3.9906. Naming the family first saves the minute.
